title: Radicals and homolytic fission
html:
Guiding question

What happens when reactants share their electrons with others?

Reactivity 3.3 looks at reactions driven by single electrons rather than electron pairs. When a covalent bond splits so that each atom keeps one of the two shared electrons, highly reactive species called radicals are formed. Radicals then grab electrons from other molecules to pair up their odd electron, setting off a chain reaction. The key example is the halogenation of alkanes in ultraviolet (UV) light.

The class "do now" links back to Structure 3.2: cracking breaks long alkanes into shorter, more useful ones (e.g. C₁₀H₂₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₂H₄), and burning alkanes releases CO₂, CO, soot and unburnt hydrocarbons. Apart from combustion and cracking, alkanes do very little; this topic is about the one reaction they do undergo readily.

CodeUnderstanding
R3.3.1A radical is a molecular entity that has an unpaired electron. Radicals are highly reactive.
R3.3.2Radicals are produced by homolytic fission, e.g. of halogens, in the presence of UV light or heat.
R3.3.3Radicals take part in substitution reactions with alkanes, producing a mixture of products.

R3.3.1 Radicals

DefinitionA radical is a molecular entity (atom, molecule or ion) that has an unpaired electron.

Radicals are shown with a dot (•) for the unpaired electron. The dot should be placed on the atom that carries the unpaired electron, for example:

  • Cl• (chlorine radical), Br• (bromine radical)
  • •CH₃ or CH₃• (methyl radical): the unpaired electron is on the carbon atom
  • •C₂H₅ (ethyl radical), •OH (hydroxyl radical), H• (hydrogen atom)
  • Stable molecules with an odd number of electrons are also radicals, e.g. nitrogen monoxide, NO•, and nitrogen dioxide, NO₂•

Why are radicals so reactive? An unpaired electron is energetically unfavourable. A radical will react with almost any molecule it meets so that its electron can pair up and form a new covalent bond. Reactions between radicals and molecules therefore have very low activation energies.

Common mistakeA radical is not the same as an ion. A chlorine radical, Cl•, has 7 valence electrons and no charge. A chloride ion, Cl⁻, has 8 valence electrons and a 1− charge. Writing Cl⁻ in a free-radical mechanism loses the mark.

You may see the older term "free radical" in past papers and older resources; it means exactly the same thing.

Which species is a radical?

  1. Cl⁻
  2. CH₄
  3. NO₂
  4. CH₃⁺

NO₂ has 5 + 6 + 6 = 17 valence electrons, an odd number, so one must be unpaired. Cl⁻ (8 valence electrons) and CH₃⁺ (6 valence electrons) are ions with all electrons paired; CH₄ is a normal molecule.

How many valence electrons does a methyl radical, •CH₃, have around its carbon atom?

  1. 6
  2. 7
  3. 8
  4. 9

Three C–H bonds supply 6 electrons, plus the single unpaired electron: 7. A carbocation CH₃⁺ would have 6; a carbanion CH₃⁻ would have 8.

R3.3.2 Homolytic fission: making radicals

DefinitionHomolytic fission is the breaking of a covalent bond in which each of the two atoms keeps one of the two bonding electrons, forming two radicals.

Homolytic fission needs an input of energy, supplied as UV light (written "hν" or "UV") or high temperature. Halogen molecules are split in this way because the two atoms are identical: neither atom pulls the shared pair more strongly, so the bond breaks evenly.

Cl₂ → 2Cl•    (UV light)
Br₂ → 2Br•    (UV light)

In a mechanism, the movement of a single electron is shown with a single-headed ("fish-hook") curly arrow. For homolytic fission of Cl–Cl, one fish-hook arrow starts in the middle of the bond and points to the left Cl, and a second points to the right Cl. A full double-headed arrow always means a pair of electrons moving (Reactivity 3.4).

Homolytic fission (R3.3)Heterolytic fission (R3.4)
What happens to the bonding pairShared out: one electron to each atomBoth electrons go to one atom
ProductsTwo radicals (no charges)A cation and an anion
Curly arrowTwo single-headed (fish-hook) arrowsOne double-headed arrow
Typical exampleCl₂ → 2Cl• in UV light(CH₃)₃C–Br → (CH₃)₃C⁺ + Br⁻
Exam tipWhy does the halogen bond break and not a C–H bond? Bond enthalpies (data booklet): Cl–Cl 242 kJ mol⁻¹ and Br–Br 193 kJ mol⁻¹, compared with C–H 414 kJ mol⁻¹. UV photons carry enough energy to break the weaker halogen–halogen bond, but not the much stronger C–H bond. (One of the older class handouts quotes 435 kJ mol⁻¹ for C–H; that is the value for the first C–H bond in methane specifically. Use the data-booklet mean, 414 kJ mol⁻¹, in IB answers.)

Link to Structure 1.3: calculate the longest wavelength of light, in nm, that can break one Cl–Cl bond (242 kJ mol⁻¹). Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

Energy per bond: E = 242 000 ÷ 6.02 × 10²³ = 4.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
λ = hc ÷ E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸) ÷ 4.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.95 × 10⁻⁷ m = 495 nm.
For C–H (414 kJ mol⁻¹) the same calculation gives about 289 nm. Sunlight at ground level contains little light below about 300 nm, so it splits Cl₂ (which absorbs most strongly in the near UV, around 330 nm) but not C–H bonds.

Which statement describes homolytic fission of Br₂?

  1. Br₂ → Br⁺ + Br⁻, shown with one double-headed arrow
  2. Br₂ → 2Br•, shown with two single-headed arrows
  3. Br₂ → 2Br⁻, needs UV light
  4. Br₂ → 2Br•, shown with one double-headed arrow

Each Br keeps one electron, giving two uncharged radicals. Each single electron's movement is drawn with its own fish-hook arrow. Ions would mean heterolytic fission.

R3.3.3 Why alkanes are unreactive

Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, and are generally very unreactive (apart from burning). There are two reasons, and an exam answer should give both:

  1. Strong bonds: C–C (346 kJ mol⁻¹) and C–H (414 kJ mol⁻¹) bonds are strong, so a lot of energy is needed to break them; reactions have high activation energies.
  2. Essentially non-polar bonds: carbon (2.6) and hydrogen (2.2) have similar electronegativities, so the C–H bond is almost non-polar. There are no δ+ or δ− sites to attract nucleophiles or electrophiles, and alkanes have no lone pairs or π bonds.

Because ionic (electron-pair) mechanisms do not work, alkanes only react with very reactive species such as radicals.

A species with an unpaired electron is called a radical; it is formed when a bond breaks by homolytic fission.

title: Free-radical substitution of alkanes
html:
R3.3.3 Free-radical substitution of alkanes

Halogenoalkanes are alkanes in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by halogen atoms. They are named by putting the halogen prefix in front of the alkane name, e.g. bromomethane, CH₃Br.

When an alkane is mixed with chlorine or bromine and exposed to UV light (sunlight), a hydrogen atom on the alkane is replaced by a halogen atom. This is free-radical substitution: a substitution reaction (one atom swapped for another) that happens by a radical mechanism.

CH₄(g) + Cl₂(g) → CH₃Cl(g) + HCl(g)    (UV light)
C₆H₁₄(g) + Br₂(g) → C₆H₁₃Br(g) + HBr(g)    (UV light)

With bromine, the orange-brown colour of bromine fades slowly in UV light, but stays in the dark. (Compare alkenes, which decolourise bromine instantly, even in the dark: R3.4.)

Hexane and bromine water are mixed in two tubes; one is kept in the dark and one is placed in sunlight. What is observed?

  1. Both decolourise immediately
  2. Only the tube in sunlight slowly loses its orange-brown colour
  3. Only the tube in the dark decolourises
  4. Neither changes colour

Light is needed to split Br₂ into radicals, so only the tube in sunlight reacts (slowly). An alkene would decolourise bromine quickly in either tube, which is how the two are told apart.

The mechanism is a chain reaction with three stages.

The mechanism: chlorination of methane

1. Initiation – radicals are created.

Cl₂ → 2Cl•

A chlorine molecule absorbs a photon of UV light with enough energy to break the Cl–Cl bond. The two identical atoms share the bonding pair equally (homolytic fission), giving two chlorine radicals.

2. Propagation – radicals are used up and regenerated (two steps).

Cl• + CH₄ → HCl + •CH₃
•CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•

In step 1 the chlorine radical removes a hydrogen atom from methane, forming hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical. In step 2 the very reactive methyl radical attacks a chlorine molecule, forming chloromethane and a new chlorine radical. That chlorine radical can repeat step 1, so one initiation event can lead to thousands of product molecules: this is why it is called a chain reaction.

3. Termination – two radicals meet and join, removing radicals from the system.

Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂
•CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl
•CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆
Key pointHow to recognise each stage from the number of radicals:
Initiation: 0 radicals on the left → 2 radicals on the right.
Propagation: 1 radical on the left → 1 radical on the right.
Termination: 2 radicals on the left → 0 radicals on the right.
Common mistakeThe step CH₄ + Cl• → CH₃Cl + H• is wrong. Hydrogen atoms (H•) are not formed in this mechanism. The first propagation step always produces the hydrogen halide (HCl or HBr) and an alkyl radical. Past-paper multiple-choice questions use this as a distractor.

Which equation is a propagation step in the bromination of ethane?

  1. Br₂ → 2Br•
  2. Br• + C₂H₆ → C₂H₅Br + H•
  3. •C₂H₅ + Br₂ → C₂H₅Br + Br•
  4. •C₂H₅ + Br• → C₂H₅Br

One radical in, one radical out: a propagation step. Br₂ → 2Br• is initiation; •C₂H₅ + Br• is termination (two radicals in, none out); the H• equation is the classic wrong step.

Classify: •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆

  1. Initiation
  2. Propagation
  3. Termination
  4. Heterolytic fission

Two radicals combine and none are left: termination. It explains why ethane appears as a by-product when methane is chlorinated.

Why a mixture of products forms

Free-radical substitution is not a clean way to make a single halogenoalkane, which is why in class we called it "not actually a very useful method". There are three reasons:

  • Further substitution: Cl• can remove a hydrogen from the product as well as from methane. CH₃Cl → CH₂Cl₂ → CHCl₃ → CCl₄. Example: Cl• + CH₃Cl → HCl + •CH₂Cl, then •CH₂Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + Cl•.
  • Termination products: two alkyl radicals joining give longer alkanes, e.g. •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆ (ethane appears as a by-product in the chlorination of methane).
  • Different hydrogens: in longer alkanes, any hydrogen can be replaced, so positional isomers form. Propane gives both 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane.

Using a large excess of the alkane makes it more likely that Cl• collides with an alkane molecule rather than a product molecule, which favours monosubstitution, but a mixture still forms.

Worked example · chlorination of ethaneWrite the mechanism for the formation of chloroethane from ethane and chlorine.
Conditions: UV light (sunlight).
Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•
Propagation 1: Cl• + C₂H₆ → •C₂H₅ + HCl
Propagation 2: •C₂H₅ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + Cl•
Termination (any one): •C₂H₅ + Cl• → C₂H₅Cl; Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •C₂H₅ + •C₂H₅ → C₄H₁₀
Check: each propagation step has one radical on each side; the two propagation steps add up to the overall equation C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl.
Worked example · bromination of a side chain1,4-dimethylbenzene, CH₃C₆H₄CH₃, reacts with bromine in UV light. The methyl groups behave like an alkane. Deduce the products when one molecule of each reacts.
Step 1: Br₂ → 2Br• (UV light, homolytic fission).
Step 2: Br• removes an H atom from a CH₃ group: Br• + CH₃C₆H₄CH₃ → HBr + CH₃C₆H₄CH₂•
Step 3: CH₃C₆H₄CH₂• + Br₂ → CH₃C₆H₄CH₂Br + Br•
Products: CH₃C₆H₄CH₂Br and HBr.
Worked example · counting monochloro isomersHow many structural isomers of C₄H₉Cl can form when butane reacts with chlorine in UV light?
Butane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃, has two kinds of hydrogen: on the end carbons (C1/C4, equivalent) and on the middle carbons (C2/C3, equivalent).
Substituting an end H gives 1-chlorobutane; substituting a middle H gives 2-chlorobutane.
Answer: 2 monochloro structural isomers (plus di-, tri-substituted products and termination products such as octane isomers).

How many monochloro structural isomers can form from pentane, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃, in UV light?

  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 4
  4. 5

By symmetry there are three kinds of H: on C1/C5, on C2/C4 and on C3. So 1-chloropentane, 2-chloropentane and 3-chloropentane.

Termination puzzle: in the chlorination of methane, which termination step gives a by-product with the formula C₂H₅Cl? Think, then reveal.•CH₂Cl + •CH₃ → CH₂ClCH₃ (chloroethane). Radicals from further substitution (•CH₂Cl) can terminate with methyl radicals, giving yet more by-products. Two •CH₂Cl radicals give CH₂ClCH₂Cl (1,2-dichloroethane).

Energy and the chain reaction

Initiation is endothermic: energy must be absorbed to break the halogen–halogen bond, which is why light (or heat) is needed. The propagation steps have very low activation energies because they involve a radical. For chlorination of methane, the overall reaction is exothermic. Using data-booklet values: bonds broken C–H (414) + Cl–Cl (242) = 656 kJ mol⁻¹; bonds formed C–Cl (324) + H–Cl (431) = 755 kJ mol⁻¹; ΔH ≈ 656 − 755 = −99 kJ mol⁻¹.

Using data-booklet bond enthalpies (C–H 414, Br–Br 193, C–Br 285, H–Br 366 kJ mol⁻¹), estimate ΔH for CH₄ + Br₂ → CH₃Br + HBr.

Bonds broken: C–H + Br–Br = 414 + 193 = 607 kJ mol⁻¹.
Bonds formed: C–Br + H–Br = 285 + 366 = 651 kJ mol⁻¹.
ΔH = 607 − 651 = −44 kJ mol⁻¹: exothermic, but less so than chlorination (−99 kJ mol⁻¹), and bromination is the slower, more selective reaction.

Light is only needed to start the chain. Once radicals form, the propagation cycle keeps going until termination removes the radicals. In practice a short burst of UV can produce a large amount of product.

Each propagation step has one radical on the left and one radical on the right; the first propagation step forms the hydrogen halide, not H•.

title: Radicals in the atmosphere and exam practice
html:
Beyond alkanes: radicals and the ozone layer

In class we applied the same ideas to chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). This is context for R3.3, not a separate syllabus statement, but it is a good test of whether you understand radical reactions.

  • High in the stratosphere, UV light breaks the weakest bond in a CFC, the C–Cl bond, by homolytic fission: CCl₂F₂ → •CClF₂ + Cl• (initiation). The C–F bond is much stronger and does not break.
  • The chlorine radical then destroys ozone in two propagation steps:
    Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂
    ClO• + O₃ → Cl• + 2O₂
  • Adding the steps: 2O₃ → 3O₂. The Cl• is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst: one chlorine radical can destroy many thousands of ozone molecules before termination.

This is why CFCs were phased out under the Montreal Protocol (the UK banned most uses by 1996), and why the ozone layer is now slowly recovering.

Exam tip"Which is the first step in the CFC-catalysed destruction of ozone?" Choose the homolytic fission of a C–Cl bond producing radicals (•CClF₂ + •Cl). Options showing ions (CClF₂⁺ + Cl⁻) describe heterolytic fission, and options breaking C–F are wrong because C–F is the strongest bond.

Why does a single chlorine radical destroy so many ozone molecules?

  1. It has a very high activation energy
  2. It is regenerated in the second propagation step, so it acts as a catalyst
  3. It forms Cl⁻ ions that react with O₃
  4. It breaks C–F bonds in other CFC molecules

Cl• is used in step 1 and re-formed in step 2, so it is not consumed overall. It keeps cycling until a termination step removes it.

Exam question (b): when chlorinated alkanes enter the upper atmosphere, C–Cl bonds are broken, producing a reactive intermediate that catalyses 2O₃ → 3O₂. (i) Name the type of intermediate. (ii) Write two equations to show how it acts as a catalyst. Answer, then reveal.(i) A (chlorine) radical. (ii) Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂ and ClO• + O₃ → Cl• + 2O₂ (either order). The mark scheme credits the dot anywhere on the radical but penalises a missing dot once.

Exam practice

Exam question (a): chloromethane reacts with chlorine to form dichloromethane. Write equations for the initiation step, the first and second propagation steps, and the termination step that forms a compound with empirical formula CH₂Cl. [4] Try it, then reveal.Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•
Propagation 1: Cl• + CH₃Cl → •CH₂Cl + HCl
Propagation 2: Cl₂ + •CH₂Cl → CH₂Cl₂ + Cl•
Termination: 2•CH₂Cl → CH₂ClCH₂Cl (1,2-dichloroethane, C₂H₄Cl₂, empirical formula CH₂Cl). Writing the molecular formula C₂H₄Cl₂ instead of the structure was penalised.
Exam question: fluorine reacts with fluoromethane (CH₃F) to form difluoromethane (CH₂F₂). Write the initiation step, both propagation steps and a termination step that gives 1,2-difluoroethane. Then write an overall equation for fluorine + ethane forming pentafluoroethane (CF₃CHF₂). Try it, then reveal.Initiation: F₂ → 2F•
Propagation 1: F• + CH₃F → •CH₂F + HF
Propagation 2: F₂ + •CH₂F → CH₂F₂ + F•
Termination: 2•CH₂F → CH₂FCH₂F
Overall: CH₃CH₃ + 5F₂ → CF₃CHF₂ + 5HF (five H atoms replaced, each producing one HF).
Charges (F⁺, F⁻) were penalised every time.

Which conditions are needed for methane to react with chlorine?

  1. Heat under reflux with a nickel catalyst
  2. UV light (or very high temperature)
  3. Aqueous sodium hydroxide
  4. Concentrated sulfuric acid

Radicals are made by homolytic fission of Cl₂, which needs UV light (sunlight) or a high temperature. "Reflux" or "catalyst" is not accepted.

Typical exam questions and how to answer them

  • "State the type of reaction and mechanism" (methane + chlorine in sunlight): substitution; free-radical (chain) mechanism. "Free-radical substitution" or "SR" scores the mark.
  • "State the conditions": UV light / sunlight / hν, or high temperature. "Reflux" or "catalyst" is not accepted.
  • "Write the initiation step": X₂ → 2X•, and say it is homolytic fission caused by UV light.
  • "Formulate two propagation steps and one termination step": follow the template above. Check that each propagation step has one radical on each side and that the propagation steps add up to the overall equation. Markschemes accept the dot anywhere on the radical, but placing it on the correct atom is good practice.
  • "Explain why a mixture of products forms": further substitution of the product, termination steps joining alkyl radicals, and substitution at different carbon atoms.
  • "Explain why alkanes are unreactive": strong C–C and C–H bonds and low bond polarity.

Summary

TermWhat to remember
RadicalSpecies with an unpaired electron; very reactive; drawn with •
Homolytic fissionEach atom keeps one electron of the bond; needs UV light or heat; fish-hook arrows
InitiationX₂ → 2X•
PropagationX• + RH → HX + R•; R• + X₂ → RX + X•
TerminationAny two radicals combining: X• + X•, R• + X•, R• + R•
Product mixtureMultiple substitution, termination by-products, positional isomers

A step in which two radicals combine and no radicals remain is called termination.
